newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Belarus economy seen hard to integrate with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Belarus economy seen hard to integrate with Russia.

text.p: Backwards Belarus, with an unreformed economy and protestors roaming its streets, is neither willing nor able to integrate quickly with its big cousin Russia, economists said on Friday.
Belarus has been edging back towards Russia for some time and President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday that the two former Soviet republics could merge, although he did not say when.
"Maybe after all this will be a single state," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as saying.
Western economists said any union would be a tough task.

"Between slow reform and no reform at all, it is difficult to say which will prevail," one said of Belarus. Russia would insist that Belarus should not leave Moscow to shoulder all the multi-billion dollar costs of union, he added.

Belarus -- Russia's western neighbour and its buffer from Eastern European nation seeking to join an enlarged NATO -- is mired in Soviet-like economic and political policy. It has been rocked by protests against President Alexander Lukashenko's near dictatorial powers and his drive for merger with Russia.
It has about a 15th of Russia's 150-million strong population but its Gross Domestic Product was only a 40th of Russia's in 1996.

Belarus's poor progress with privatisation caused both the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to break off relations, although both have made overtures in the past month and said they would return to the capital Minsk if reforms began.
Lukashenko has stressed the need for Belarus to keep its sovereignty in union with Russia. Although many Belarussians support closer ties with Moscow, few want complete union.
Economists say in reality Russia would take over Belarus although the idea is called a merger. But for Russia, which is struggling to reverse its own economic decline, the cost might be unaffordable.
One Western economist compared Belarus's economy with that of Russia's poorest regions, where factories stand idle.

Belarus owes Russia millions of dollars for gas and oil, and has virtually no privatisation. The artificially-supported currency, the Belarussian rouble, trades at a 30 percent discount in Moscow from its value in Minsk.
The Western analyst said a straight swap of Belarussian roubles for Russian roubles would cost five percent of Russian GDP.
"Economic union is not at all fiscally possible in the short term," said Keith Darden, a scholar of the University of California at Berkeley.

"Belarus and Russia would have to integrate their economic policy and Belarus has not even started privatisation," said Darden, who specialises in integration among the Commonwealth of Independent States, which includes all the former Soviet republics except the Baltics.

Yeltsin made clear to Lukashenko in January that integration would not proceed until Belarus lived up to previous agreements to synchronise customs policies. Alcohol and other imports pour through Belarus into Russia, missing the Russian treasury which needs customs duties from the trade.
Belarussian industry, known abroad for tractors that barely run, television sets that break down and refrigerators resembling squat boxes, has barely any privatised companies.
Profits tax receipts contracted 40 percent last year, although industrial output grew 3.2 percent. The economy has contracted 35 percent from 1991 levels.
Lukashenko has made it clear changes will be slow.
"Why must we synchronise with the Russian (reform) example?" he told the Russian Duma lower house of parliament on Tuesday. "(Instead) we can offer Russia our example of privatisation."
